questions.question: Why is chunking necessary for RAG systems using most embedding models?
options: Models have a limited context window and lose detail in long documents.
Chunking makes the documents look better in the UI.
It is a required step for all vector databases.
It removes stop words from the text.
questions.explanation: Embedding models (like BERT) typically only see 512 tokens. Even long-context models struggle to compress a whole book into one vector without losing the specific details needed for RAG.

questions.question: According to 2026 benchmarks, which chunking strategy is often the best default?
options: Recursive chunking (splitting on paragraph, then sentence, then word).
questions.explanation: Recursive chunking balances performance and coherence by trying to split text at natural boundaries (like double newlines) before falling back to smaller units.

questions.question: What is the 'parent-document' pattern in chunking?
options: Retrieving small child chunks but providing the larger parent context to the LLM.
Only indexing the first page of every document.
Using the document's metadata instead of its content.
Letting the LLM decide where to split the document.
questions.explanation: Small chunks are better for precise retrieval, but the LLM often needs the surrounding context (the parent section) to generate a complete and accurate answer.

questions.question: What is the 'context cliff' observed in 2026 RAG research?
options: A sharp drop in response quality around 2,500 context tokens.
When a model stops generating text completely.
When the retriever fails to find any documents.
When the vector database runs out of memory.
questions.explanation: Adding more context is not always better. Researchers found that providing too many retrieved chunks can distract the model, leading to a drop in accuracy around 2.5k tokens.
